So I assume it depends on what you train.

- Exact problems on benchmark.

- Similar problems to benchmark.

- Broad class of problems or techniques that might apply to benchmark

Each has very different ramifications for how the model performs. The current evidence is that Anthropic and OpenAI is generally operating lower in the list.

I’m pretty sure “benchmaxxing” as defined is a standard post-training procedure for ALL models.

One can argue though some models are post-trained heavily for specific benchmarks and less for other datasets. So they are weaker on out of distribution tasks.

Benchmaxing is defined as targeted post-training attempts to optimise for higher benchmarks. This doesn’t change the aggregate intelligence or capability of the model, so it can make a model appear more capable than it is.

Neither is the primary cause, I suspect. If you look at the coding index alone, you see more plausible results from a software engineering perspective (in particular, Terra no longer outperforming Fable) [1].

That especially the small flash models that are primarily optimized for coding tasks would perform worse at non-coding tasks is not per se surprising to me. The introduction of Terminal-Bench Science 0.1 in particular hurts their aggregate scores [2].

The general question remains of how meaningful aggregating the results of very heterogeneous tasks into a single numeric score is. (Aside from general questions about individual benchmark validity.)

Note: the cyber index is also interesting. While refusals make it somewhat opaque, even if you optimistically count all refusals for Opus and Fable as successes, the results are ... fascinating [3].

I'll add that I really want to know how Opus 4.x and Codex 5.x perform on the new index. Once we have that information, this is going to give us a better understanding of how meaningful the scores are.

children.author: yorwba
children.text:
Their problem is really that individual benchmarks are not that informative. Bad enough models all perform at chance level, good enough models all saturate the benchmark. And the number of tasks is often low enough that differences of several percentage points might just be noise. Artificial Analysis' approach of aggregating scores in a weighted sum is largely just choosing which noise to amplify more.

I prefer Epoch's https://epoch.ai/eci methodology as they explicitly model benchmark saturation and also provide error bars for their estimates.

children.author: hgoel
children.text:
I was a little suspicious last time, but even moreso this time. The slant their scores take, and the release timing is very suspect. On the other hand, new models drop on a near daily basis, so maybe there's no way to appear entirely fair.

An issue I think all benchmarks suffer from is regarding precision. What does a one point difference mean? How many points of difference is needed to translate into a meaningful distinction between models?

Among fellow humans, we often find ourselves picking what we consider to be most intelligent and then designing the tests around that. I've noticed a similar thing in AI, where whatever OAI/Anthropic decide to focus on improving becomes the new measure of intelligence. With their latest models, this seems to be 3d modeling/game making capabilities. Unsurprisingly, because that isn't what the Chinese companies have been focusing on, they appear behind on "frontier" reasoning tests. On top of that, older tests end up being discarded for being saturated. Makes me think that maybe unintentionally, the methodology used for these scores might be biased towards Western companies.

This would also fit with the widely discussed decline in writing quality from Opus and the worse readability of code produced by one of OAI's recent models, despite benchmarks continuing to show progress on all fronts.

Plus, if they're going to update the benchmark so frequently to discard saturated components, is there even a research-related point to keeping it private?
